title: The Week Capitec Listed, Days After Saambou Bank Collapsed
dek: Michiel le Roux and Riaan Stassen turned a group of cash-loan shops into a bank for South Africans the big banks served badly, and listed it in the middle of a banking crisis.

story.founder: Michiel le Roux and Riaan Stassen
story.event: Building a low-cost bank from micro-lenders and listing it during a banking crisis
story.summary: Michiel le Roux, former head of Boland Bank, agreed with the PSG group to turn its micro-lending shops into a bank for lower-income South Africans, recruiting Riaan Stassen and other Boland managers in 2000; the bank opened in 2001 as Daxacom and became Capitec. It listed on the JSE on 18 February 2002, days after Saambou Bank collapsed, and its shares fell from R2.75 to 80 cents; after cutting loan rates by about 40% the founders had to put in their own cash, but the bank survived and by 2016 had 7.3 million active clients.
paragraphs: On Monday 18 February 2002, Capitec Bank's shares began trading on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange. It was, Michiel le Roux said later, "a terrible time to list a bank." Saambou Bank had collapsed days before. Capitec's shares, expected to open at about R3, opened at R2.75 and later fell as low as 80 cents.

Le Roux, a law graduate who had worked at the liquor company Distillers and then run Boland Bank in Cape Town, had come to see banking as archaic. He had assumed, he said, that a law made banks close at half past three, and found there was none. When the investment group PSG asked him to look at the micro-lenders it had bought, he refused at first: it was "a terrible business" that charged exorbitant interest. Visiting its branches changed his mind. He concluded that the big banks served lower-income South Africans badly, and decided to build a bank for them.

PSG held the licence of a failed bank, without which, Le Roux said, he did not know if they could ever have got one. In 2000 he brought over much of Boland's senior management, among them Riaan Stassen, a former Distillers colleague. Cash-loan shops became the branch network. The bank opened in 2001 as Daxacom, a name that, after about three branches, "didn't work", and became Capitec. Le Roux told shareholders it would be "a big success or a small failure." The founders did not fully agree on whom it was for: Le Roux has described a bank for low-income people, while Stassen argued for one "for everyone".

At one stage in those founding years the bank cut its loan rates by about 40 per cent, which meant it needed 40 per cent more loans to break even. "In the first month, we made a loss, and in the second, we ran out of money," Le Roux said. The founders put in their own cash. A fund manager told them they would "never, ever, ever make it"; a bank manager called them "a bunch of loan sharks".
Capitec survived. Stassen succeeded Le Roux as chief executive in 2004 and led the bank until 2013. By 2016 it had 7.3 million active clients and 720 branches.

quote.text: Howbeit with a man in poor estate be longsuffering; and let him not wait for thine alms. Help a poor man for the commandment’s sake; and according to his need send him not empty away.
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Ben Sira treats help for the poor as a duty owed without waiting, not a loan priced to break even. Capitec's cheaper credit was still credit, and Le Roux's first instinct about micro-lending was close to Ben Sira's. A bank that must earn a return cannot simply give, and the old text does not pretend otherwise.

reflection: Le Roux's first answer to PSG was no, and for a decent reason: the business charged poor people too much. He changed his mind only after seeing the branches for himself, and then built something meant to charge them less. The discomfort did not vanish; it became the design brief.

You will meet work that looks wrong from a distance. It is worth going to see it before deciding, and worth keeping the objection you started with, written down, so that it can keep shaping what you build. Some of the best constraints are the misgivings you had on the first day.
invitation: Write down one objection you once had to a part of your own work. Ask yourself whether you have answered it, or only stopped noticing it.

cross_checks.claim: Capitec listed on the JSE on 18 February 2002
The listing came days after Saambou Bank collapsed, and the shares fell well below their opening price
Le Roux, formerly of Boland Bank, founded Capitec with Riaan Stassen and other Boland managers, backed by PSG's micro-lenders and banking licence
Le Roux saw conventional banking as archaic and set out to serve lower-income South Africans
Stassen succeeded Le Roux as chief executive

research_notes: Listing date: Forbes Africa (2016) and Profile's Stock Exchange Handbook give 18 February 2002; Stellenbosch Visio (2021) prints 18 September 2002 but also says it was nine days after Saambou's collapse, which fits February, so September is treated as a misprint. Forbes says the Reserve Bank closed Saambou 'on a Saturday' before the Monday listing; other reports say nine days or two weeks before, so the story says 'days before'. Share price: Stellenbosch Visio gives an expected R3, an opening R2.75 and a low of 80 cents; Business Day's standfirst (2019) says the founders launched the bank 'at R2 a share', which may refer to an earlier or unbundling price; the story uses the Visio figures. Founding date: Profile records incorporation on 23 November 1999 and registration as a bank controlling company on 29 June 2001, Wikipedia gives 1 March 2001 for the bank's registration, and Pretoria News says 2001; the story says the bank opened in 2001. Wikipedia lists Jannie Mouton of PSG as a third founder; the slate and most sources name Le Roux and Stassen, and the story credits PSG's backing. The date of the 40% rate cut and cash shortfall is given by Le Roux only as 'during the founding phases', so the story does not date it. Le Roux's 'big success or small failure' and banking-hours remarks were made in a radio interview reported by Pretoria News; the 702 original is no longer online. Business Day's article body is paywalled, so it is cited only for its headline and standfirst. Funding is set to mixed: PSG's backing, public shareholders from 2002 and the founders' own cash. Client numbers (7.3 million active clients, 720 branches) are Forbes Africa's 2016 figures. Ben Sira's counsel concerns almsgiving and is applied by analogy to lending to the poor.
